VI. THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN LOCAL SHORT-TERM USES OF MAN'S ENVIRONMENT AND THE MAINTENANCE AND ENHANCEMENT OF LONG-TERM PRODUCTIVITY
A justifiable concern with any major public improvement is that future generations and the future economy could be burdened with the environmental costs of a project designed for short-term benefits. The proposed action will tend toward the opposite effect. While most of the costs and inconveniences involved will be borne during or shortly after construction, the benefits will be shared by both present and future generations.
A. Short-term Effect
The effect that this facility could have is on the short-term productivity. The short-term productivity effect would be a continued accelerated progression involving regional and community growth in accordance with adopted land-use plans, policies, goals, and objectives.
In metropolitan area, land-use changes are related to the local and regional planning goals and objectives contained in published comprehensive plans. The local and regional planning goals are usually taken as a time span of 20 to 25 years (one generation). The highway design year is also compatible with this time (20 years) and is related to the trip generations for the land-use described in adopted local and regional plans. With the short-term effect fully recognized; the investment in freeway right-of-way and freeway structures could be considered a long-term effect since these investments are usually predicted on 100 years (about four generations) and 50 years (about two generations) life spans respectively. Therefore, it could further be considered that any changes including upgrading of the transportation facilities within the freeway right-of-way constitutes a short-term effect. In this context, "short-term use of man's environment" is taken to mean the period of construction and operation of the facility within the rights-of-way.
The construction will have a short-term impact upon the community business areas. There will be some loses involved to the businesses directly implicated. However, access to all faciliites; business, commercial and residential; will be maintained during the various construction stages in order to minimize the affect.
The State Relocation Assistance and Payment Program will be administered to offset any appreciable loss to the affected businesses. Six businesses and two residential structures will need to be acquired resulting from the implementation of this improvement.
